parts.title: Why Does This Magnet FLOAT? Two Poles, a Pull and a Push (Part 1) | Magnet Poles
parts.description:
Two ring magnets on a pencil, and the top one floats in mid-air. What holds it up, a pull or a push? Lock in your answer from last time, be the top ring magnet and feel the push, find out where a magnet pulls the hardest, and spot Pip's mistake about the floating ring. Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Properties of Magnets: magnet poles.

In this part:
• Two ring magnets on a pencil: what holds up the top one? (last episode's dare)
• Be the top ring magnet: a push you cannot see
• Look closer: where is a magnet strongest? The two poles
• Every magnet has two poles, whatever its shape
• HOLD ON! The floating ring will not come down. Is it broken?
• Look closer: pull or push? Two magnets on round pencils
• Spot the hidden spider!

Key words: poles, attraction, repel.
Watch Part 2: like poles, unlike poles, and how to prove something is a magnet. Last episode: why a magnet ignores a copper wire.

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies!

Why does a ring magnet float in mid-air? P3 Science, Chapter 6, Properties of Magnets (pp. 105 to 109): a magnet has two poles, a North pole and a South pole, where attraction is the strongest; magnets can attract (pull) or repel (push) one another; unlike poles attract and like poles repel; and you can confirm that an object is a magnet if it repels another magnet. The second episode of the Magnets theme. Also fits US NGSS 3-PS2-3 (Grade 3).
Safety and care: Keep magnets away from phones, cards and little brothers and sisters, and never put a magnet in your mouth. Ask an adult before you borrow things from the toolbox. We look at spiders and lizards, and we do not touch them.
Try it at home: With an adult, use two bar magnets or two round whiteboard magnets. Turn one round and feel the pull change into a push. (Flat fridge magnets with pictures on them do not show this well.)
Dip a magnet into the steel paper clips from your class stationery tray: they bunch at the two poles. Whiteboard magnets in your classroom have two poles too. Floating-magnet toys from a bookshop float because like poles repel.
Grade 3 pupils in the US learn it the same way (NGSS 3-PS2-3): magnets can push and pull without touching, and which way depends on which poles face each other.
